title: Population growth, fertility and population policy

parts.label: A

rubric.point: Gives the average number of children a woman has, or would have, over her lifetime.
accept: Average number of births per woman in her lifetime
Average number of children per woman if a year’s birth rates stay the same

parts.sample: The total fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have over her lifetime if the birth rates of one year stayed the same.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Identify the TFR known as replacement-level fertility in a country where few children die.

rubric.point: Gives about 2.1 births per woman (replacement level).
accept: About 2.1
About two children per woman, a little over 2

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain why a country’s population can keep growing for several decades after its TFR falls below replacement level.

rubric.point: Explains that a large number of young people from earlier high fertility are now at childbearing age, so births still exceed deaths for a time.
accept: Many young adults from past high fertility still have children, so births exceed deaths
A young age structure keeps births above deaths (population momentum)
A young population keeps deaths low while many couples still have children, so births exceed deaths

parts.sample: Because years of high fertility left a very large number of young people, many couples are now at childbearing age, so even with fewer children each, total births stay above deaths for decades.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Describe one pronatalist policy that a government has used. Name the country.

rubric.point: Describes a real policy meant to raise births (what it gives or requires) and names the country.
accept: Hungary (2019): loans cancelled after a third child
France or Sweden: family payments, paid parental leave, cheap child care
Singapore (1987): urging families to have three or more children
China (2021): three-child policy with child care support
Romania (1966): ban on most abortions

parts.sample: Hungary, from 2019, offers young married couples a large loan that is cancelled once they have a third child, so the policy rewards families for having more children.

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: Explain one reason a pronatalist policy may have only a small effect on a country’s TFR.

rubric.point: Explains a reason with its link, such as payments being small next to the costs of raising children, so couples still choose small families.
accept: Payments are small compared with the cost of housing, schooling and child care, so couples still have few children
Women’s jobs and long work hours make large families hard, so incentives change little
Cultural norms favor small families, so money does not change choices
Effects are temporary: births are moved earlier, not increased

parts.sample: Payments are small compared with the costs of housing, schooling and child care, so many couples still decide to have one or two children; South Korea spent heavily after 2006, yet its TFR fell to 0.72 in 2023 (Statistics Korea, 2024).

parts.label: F
parts.prompt: Compare the goal of China’s one-child policy (1980 to 2015) with the goal of its three-child policy (2021).

rubric.point: States both goals: the one-child policy aimed to lower births and slow growth, while the three-child policy aimed to raise births.
accept: One-child: lower births, slow growth; three-child: raise births as fertility fell
Antinatalist then pronatalist

parts.sample: The one-child policy aimed to lower births and slow population growth, whereas the three-child policy aimed to raise births, because by 2021 fertility was far below replacement and the population was getting older.

parts.label: G
parts.prompt: Explain the degree to which a national TFR describes fertility in every region of a large country, such as India.

rubric.point: States a degree and explains that a national average hides differences between regions at the subnational scale.
accept: To a limited degree: the national figure is an average that hides regional differences (for example Kerala and Bihar)
To a small degree: data at the state or local scale are needed

parts.sample: To a limited degree. The national TFR is an average for the whole country, so it hides large differences between states, such as much lower fertility in Kerala than in Bihar (National Family Health Survey, 2019-21); data at the subnational scale are needed to see them.
